transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:37 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Lina Park (CSM), Raj Patel (Apex CTO), Hannah Lee (Apex ML Eng), Marcus V. (Infra), Sofia Gomez (Security)

Summary: quick discovery focused on p95 latency targets, concurrency, streaming needs and benchmarking tokens/sec. Apex is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC) for a real-time inference use case (customer-facing recommendations + chat).

Topics: p95 targets, concurrency, batching, streaming responses, token/sec bench details, KV cache, quantization tradeoffs, security and SSO/KMS concerns.

----- Transcript -----
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. were you able to see the invite notes? uh just to confirm, today we'll run through your latency/throughput goals, typical concurrency and then outline next steps for a benchmark.
[00:10] Raj Patel: yeah thanks Maya. this is Raj. um our main ask right now is we need p95 < 250ms for short chat turns (~64 tokens) for our web UI, and for longer generations we want predictable token/sec when streaming.
[00:22] Hannah Lee: and to add, we need to support spikes to ~150 concurrent users hitting the chat endpoint, so effective concurrent inference windows probably look like 40-60 concurrent requests with burst to 150.
[00:33] Marcus V.: our current stack is a mix of managed infra, we have k8s clusters in GCP and some on-prem for sensitive data. we're evaluating hosted first but might need a VPC/private option because of data residency and our security team.
[00:44] Diego Ruiz: got it. quick clarification — when you say p95 < 250, is that for end-to-end from client to model response or just model inference p95?
[00:49] Raj Patel: model inference p95, yes. we can add network delta separately but want the model to be under 250ms for the majority of short turns.
[00:55] Diego Ruiz: okay that's helpful. so for short prompts (<=64 tokens) on modern open models, on dedicated GPU pools we typically see model-side p95 in the 60-200ms range depending on quantization and batching. On hosted multi-tenant there is a bit more variance, especially at tail.
[01:10] Hannah Lee: can you explain batching impact? we worried about batching hurting latency for chat.
[01:14] Diego Ruiz: absolutely. there are two axes — request-level latency and throughput. continuous batching and smart prefetching can amortize cost, but if you set strict p95 SLOs, you tune batch windows smaller or use dedicated capacity. Redwood's runtime supports workload-aware batching and dynamic policies. in practice for chat we often keep batch windows low (5-10ms) and leverage KV cache for prefix reuse to keep p95 low.
[01:34] Raj Patel: what about streaming? we need streaming tokens as they are generated — p50 token latency matters for perceived responsiveness. what's your tokens/sec under streaming for say a 2k token response?
[01:45] Diego Ruiz: streaming has two parts: generation latency per token and network/flush behavior. on a 2k seq with optimized kernels and good batching you might see sustained ~200-500 tokens/sec depending on model size and quantization. for p50 token latency we often see single-digit-ms per token on the fast path, but p95 token latency can spike if there's a scheduling conflict or KV cache miss.
[02:06] Marcus V.: can you run numbers for 8k sequence? our long-form reports can go up to 8k. also concurrency for that workload will be lower — maybe 5-10 concurrent long sessions.
[02:15] Diego Ruiz: 8k changes the kernel selection and memory paths, yes. on 8k you'll want model variants optimized for long context (and usually dedicated or private pools). tokens/sec drops relative to short seq; for 8k we often measure token/sec in the ~30-120 tokens/sec range on a single-shot generation depending on hardware and quantization. again dedicated pools give more predictable tails.
[02:32] Hannah Lee: you mentioned quantization — we are open to 4-bit quant but concerned about accuracy. how much latency gain vs quality loss typically?
[02:39] Diego Ruiz: quantization to 4-bit often reduces latency 20-40% and halves memory footprint; however quality impact depends on model and prompts. Redwood Optimize can run A/B evals and a regression alert if output quality drops. We usually recommend an eval set from customers — we'll run quant-aware benchmarks and show cost/latency tradeoffs.
[02:59] Sofia Gomez: from security side — we need SOC2, KMS integration, audit logs, SSO and RBAC, and a VPC option. does Redwood Hosted support customer-managed KMS?
[03:08] Maya Chen: yes, hosted with dedicated tenancy supports customer-managed keys and audit logs; private deployment (VPC) gives the most control. i'll share the SOC2/ISO packs and the VPC network diagram after the call.
[03:18] Raj Patel: great. one more — how do fallbacks work in case dedicated pool is saturated? we need graceful degradation.
[03:23] Diego Ruiz: smart routing — requests can fail over to a compatible model variant (possibly lower-cost quantized variant) or to another region depending on policy. Redwood Console shows per-route SLOs so you can tune fallback thresholds. we also support canary rollouts and automatic fallback policies.
[03:36] Hannah Lee: can you outline the benchmark you'd run for us? especially tokens/sec and p95 for 64-token chat and 8k long-form.
[03:42] Diego Ruiz: proposed benchmark: 1) chat test: 64-token prompts, concurrency sweep 1,8,16,32,64,128 with streaming on; measure p50/p95 model inference latency and tokens/sec while varying batch window and with KV cache warm/cold. 2) long-form test: 2k and 8k seqs, concurrency 1-16, measure tokens/sec and memory/GC events; 3) stability run: 2 hour sustained 64-concurrency chat to surface tails. we'll collect traces and flamegraphs and share raw logs.
[04:09] Raj Patel: sounds good. what hardware would you use for the dedicated run? we prefer A100-class nodes but also want to compare to cheaper options.
[04:16] Diego Ruiz: we can run on our Dedicated GPU pools (A100 and H100 if available) and provide per-node metrics. we can also test with quantized CPU fallback for cost comparison but that won't hit your p95 targets.
[04:26] Maya Chen: recap of immediate next steps: we'll send pricing doc and SOC2/VPC docs; Diego will prepare benchmark scripts; Hannah will send sample prompts and p95 targets; schedule the technical deep dive for next week.
[04:37] Raj Patel: ok thanks — can you include an example dashboard screenshot for tracing and token-level cost in the docs?
[04:42] Lina Park: yes i'll attach Redwood Console screenshots showing per-route token cost and latency heatmaps.
[04:46] Sofia Gomez: also include network egress assumptions for hosted vs VPC.
[04:50] Maya Chen: noted. any other questions?
[04:53] Hannah Lee: one small thing — for the benchmark please surface model jitter (stddev) and score latency percentiles up to p99.9 if possible.
[04:59] Diego Ruiz: absolutely. we'll include p50/p90/p95/p99/p99.9, plus tokens/sec distribution.
[05:04] Raj Patel: thanks all. we'll review docs and get the sample prompts over today.
[05:07] Maya Chen: great — thanks everyone. we'll follow up by EOD with the docs and proposed dates for the deep dive.

End of transcript.
